insights.claim: TrustyAI Explainability has no application-level authentication on any HTTP endpoint, making access control entirely dependent on platform-level enforcement (OpenShift Route, NetworkPolicy, or service mesh).
insights.reasoning: No JAX-RS security annotations (@RolesAllowed, @Authenticated) or SecurityContext injection found across all endpoint classes. The OpenShift Route has tls: null, exposing plaintext HTTP. The consumer endpoint at /consumer/kserve/v2 accepts arbitrary inference payloads without authentication, relying on network-level isolation. This is a safety-critical gap if the platform does not enforce network segmentation.

insights.claim: The RHOAI distribution profile disables all explainer endpoints (SHAP, LIME, Counterfactual, TSSaliency, global) via Quarkus feature flags, reducing the API surface to only fairness and drift monitoring.
insights.reasoning: The RHOAI profile in application.properties explicitly sets all explainer endpoint flags to 'disable' while enabling fairness and drift. This uses Quarkus @EndpointDisabled annotations for compile-time endpoint gating, ensuring a clean distribution-specific API surface without code forking.

insights.claim: The init container creates a model-serving-config ConfigMap that couples TrustyAI to the KServe/ModelMesh payload processing pipeline, requiring the trustyai-serviceaccount to have cluster-wide ConfigMap CRUD permissions.
insights.reasoning: The init container uses oc apply to create a ConfigMap pointing KServe payload processors to the TrustyAI consumer endpoint. This requires a ClusterRole with full ConfigMap CRUD verbs and a ClusterRoleBinding to trustyai-serviceaccount. The trade-off is operational simplicity (automatic registration) versus elevated RBAC scope (cluster-wide ConfigMap write access).
